title: Directed graphs and order
sub: Course Schedule: Kahn's algorithm and three colors; Clone Graph: an old → new dictionary
cards/0/title: Course Schedule: dependencies are a directed graph
cards/0/body:
Course Schedule (LeetCode #207). Up to 2000 courses numCourses and up to 5000 pairs prerequisites; the pair [a, b] means “to take a, first complete b”. Can you finish all the courses?

Signals: “depends on”, “first — then”, “build, load or initialization order”. This is a directed graph: the edge b → a means “b is needed for a”. You can finish everything exactly when the graph has no cycle: courses on a cycle wait for each other forever. An order in which every edge points forward is called topological.

The graph comes as an edge list — move it into adjacency lists, List<int>[], in O(V + E). At the same time count each vertex's in-degree: how many prerequisites the course has.

How a directed graph differs from a grid. In lesson 1, meeting an already visited cell meant nothing. Here, too, not every repeat meeting is a cycle: in the “diamond” 0 → 1 → 3 and 0 → 2 → 3, vertex 3 is reached twice, yet there is no cycle.
cards/1/q: Which problems need a topological order or cycle detection in a directed graph? Select all.
cards/1/options/0: The build order of projects, each referencing others
cards/1/options/1: Whether all quests can be completed when quests have required predecessors
cards/1/options/2: The number of connected regions on a tile map
cards/1/options/3: The distance from every cell to the nearest exit
cards/1/options/4: The recalculation order of spreadsheet cells whose formulas refer to other cells
cards/1/explain: Builds, quests and formulas are all “this first, then that”: directed dependency edges, where a cycle makes the task impossible. Connected regions are undirected connectivity (lesson 1), and the distance to an exit is a multi-source BFS (lesson 2): no order is needed there.
cards/2/title: Kahn's algorithm: take whatever is already possible
cards/2/body:
A course's in-degree is the number of its unmet prerequisites. Courses with in-degree 0 can be taken right away — they go into the queue. Take a course from the queue: taken++, and every course that depends on it loses 1 from its in-degree. Whoever reaches 0 joins the queue.

Invariant: a course enters the queue only once all its prerequisites have been taken. So the order in which courses leave the queue is topological.

Why the leftovers are a cycle. If the queue is empty but taken < n, every remaining course has in-degree above 0 and is waiting for another remaining course. Walk from a course to its unmet prerequisite, from that one to its prerequisite… There are finitely many courses, so the walk closes — that's a cycle. Kahn doesn't loop forever: the courses of a cycle simply never enter the queue.

Cost: every vertex enters the queue once and every edge decrements an in-degree once — O(V + E) time and memory.
cards/3/explain: The pair [a, b] means “a requires b”, the edge b → a: p[0] goes into the list next[p[1]], and p[0]'s in-degree grows. Courses without prerequisites start. The prefix decrement --indegree[d] compares the already decremented value with zero; the postfix indegree[d]-- would compare the old one and miss the moment the in-degree became 0. The queue is always empty at the end — the answer comes from the taken counter.
cards/4/task: Courses 0–5: a diamond 0 → 1, 2 → 3, then 3 → 4 → 5, plus an edge 5 → 3 — course 3 also requires course 5. Badges show how many prerequisites a course is still waiting for. The rig will ask twice what the code does.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Course 3 will have 2 prerequisites left — it won't enter the queue
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Course 3 enters the queue: one of its prerequisites is done
cards/4/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Course 3 is taken right after 1: it's next by number
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: Course 1 is about to be taken — one of course 3's prerequisites. What happens to course 3?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: Course 3 has three prerequisites — 1, 2 and 5 — so its badge is 3. Taking course 1 brings it down to 2. Only courses whose in-degree reaches zero enter the queue: one met prerequisite isn't enough. The course number doesn't set the order — the queue does.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: false: courses 3, 4 and 5 wait for each other in a circle
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: true: everything that could be taken was taken
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: Course 2 is taken and the queue is empty; 3 of 6 courses are taken. What does the code return?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: taken = 3, while n = 6. Course 3 still has a badge of 1 (waiting for 5), course 4 has 1 (waiting for 3), course 5 has 1 (waiting for 4): none of them will reach zero — that is the cycle 3 → 4 → 5 → 3. Kahn can't loop forever: the courses of a cycle simply never enter the queue, and the while loop ends.
cards/5/body:
The second way to find a cycle is DFS, but with three vertex states. White (0): not visited yet. Gray (1): the vertex is on the current recursion path — we entered it and haven't left. Black (2): fully explored, no cycle leads out of it.

An edge into a gray vertex points back to an ancestor on the current path — that's a cycle. An edge into a black one isn't: in the diamond, vertex 3 turns black after the branch through 1, and the branch through 2 simply skips it. Two states aren't enough: a plain visited can't tell “I'm on this path” from “I was here earlier via another branch” and finds a cycle in the diamond.

Order. A vertex turns black after all its descendants. If you record vertices as they turn black, you get a topological order in reverse — reverse it, and you have the answer to Course Schedule II (#210).

Depth: up to V frames. For 2000 courses that's safe; for 10⁵ nodes use Kahn or an explicit stack (lesson 1). Time is O(V + E), the same as Kahn.
cards/6/q: On the diamond n = 4, [[1,0],[2,0],[3,1],[3,2]] this code finds a cycle, though there is none. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/6/explain: HasCycle(0) goes to 1 and from there to 3: 3 has no edges, so it returns. Then 0 goes to 2, and 2 sees visited[3] = true and declares a cycle. But 3 isn't on the current path 0 → 2 — it was finished earlier, via another branch. Three states are needed: only an edge into a gray vertex is a cycle, and a black one is skipped.
cards/7/title: Order in a game: systems, bundles, tech trees
cards/7/body:
System initialization. [DefaultExecutionOrder] and Script Execution Order in the project settings give MonoBehaviours an order by hand, with numbers. When there are thirty services, each with declared dependencies, Kahn produces the order, and on a cycle a clear error listing the stuck ones: the cycle and everything that depends on it. Entities does the same: systems inside a group are sorted by [UpdateBefore] and [UpdateAfter], and a cycle makes the sort fail with an error.

Bundles. AssetBundleManifest.GetAllDependencies(name) returns all of a bundle's dependencies, direct and indirect. Unity doesn't care in which order the bundles themselves are loaded: what matters is that the dependencies are loaded before you load an asset from the bundle that needs them. Addressables does this for you. Kahn belongs in the build script here — to check that the bundle graph has no cycle.

Tech trees. A technology becomes available when all its prerequisites are researched — that's in-degree 0. Research one, and its dependents lose 1: Kahn stretched over a whole match.

Waves. Kahn by levels, with queue.Count at the start of a level as in u10.l1: a level is the set of systems that can be initialized in parallel, and the number of levels is the length of the longest dependency chain (Parallel Courses, #1136).

Determinism. The order from a Queue depends on the order of the input. If you need a stable one, “ascending id”, use a min-heap instead of the queue: PriorityQueue in .NET 6+, SortedSet<int> in Unity. The cost is O(V log V + E): each vertex enters and leaves the heap once, and edges still cost O(1).
cards/7/deep:
Showing the cycle itself. The list of stuck nodes is the cycle plus everything depending on it. To print exactly the cycle you need DFS with three colors and a path stack: when you meet a gray vertex d, the cycle is the stack's vertices from d to the current one.

Kahn or DFS. Both are O(V + E). Kahn has no recursion, yields levels naturally and is easy to make incremental (the tech tree). DFS is shorter for “is there a cycle” and finds the cycle right away. For an order with the smallest id first only Kahn with a heap works — DFS gives some valid order, but not the lexicographically smallest one.

Bundle dependencies. It pays to check the dependency graph in the build script with the same Kahn. A cycle between bundles means they can only live in memory together: unload one and the other loses assets it references. It usually signals that a shared asset should move into a bundle of its own.

Unity and Awake order. The order of Awake calls between objects in one scene is not guaranteed unless you set it. An explicit service dependency graph plus a single bootstrap object that initializes them in topological order is the usual answer to “how is your bootstrap built”.
cards/8/q: A system loader: dependencies are known, and everything that doesn't depend on each other should initialize in parallel, in waves. How do you find the waves, and how many will there be?
cards/8/options/0: Kahn by levels: take queue.Count at a time; there are as many waves as the longest dependency chain
cards/8/options/1: DFS with three colors: as many waves as vertices that turn black
cards/8/options/2: As many waves as systems without dependencies: each one opens its own wave
cards/8/options/3: One wave: Kahn gives an order, and the order is a single wave
cards/8/explain: A Kahn level is all systems whose dependencies were finished on earlier levels, and they don't depend on each other. A system lands on level k if the longest chain leading to it is k steps, so there are as many levels as the longest chain.
cards/8/wrong/1: Every vertex turns black, so that's just n. Colors find cycles; they don't separate levels.
cards/8/wrong/2: The systems without dependencies all form the first wave. After that, the chain lengths decide the waves.
cards/8/wrong/3: Kahn's order is sequential: inside it, systems of one level simply stand next to each other. The waves become visible only if you take a whole level at a time.
cards/9/title: Clone Graph: an old → new dictionary
cards/9/body:
Clone Graph (LeetCode #133). You get a node of a connected undirected graph (up to 100 nodes): a Node with a value and a list of neighbors. Return a deep copy — new nodes with the same connections.

Two traps. Cycles: an undirected edge is a reference in both directions, and a naive “copy the neighbors” recursion runs in circles forever. Shared neighbors: if two nodes point to a third, the copy must also have one third node, not two.

A Dictionary<Node, Node> “original → copy” solves both. It is both visited and the way to find a copy that already exists. The key rule: put the copy into the dictionary before visiting the neighbors. Then a neighbor that points back finds the ready copy. Time is O(V + E). Node doesn't override Equals, so keys are compared by reference — exactly what we want.

In Unity this is how Object.Instantiate works: when an object is copied with all its children, references inside the copied hierarchy are redirected to the copies, while references pointing outside stay as they were. You need the same dictionary when copying a graph stored in ScriptableObjects — dialogues, quests, behavior nodes.
cards/10/task: Step through copying the square 1 — 2 — 3 — 4 — 1 with BFS and an old → new dictionary. The rig asks twice what the code does with the next neighbor: create a copy or only add a reference.
cards/10/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Only a reference: 1′ exists — add it to the neighbors of 2′
cards/10/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Creates another copy of 1 and puts 1 into the queue
cards/10/goal/asks/0/options/2/label: Nothing: 1 is processed, the edge 1 — 2 is already copied
cards/10/goal/asks/0/q: 2 has been taken; 1′, 2′ and 4′ are already in the dictionary. The first neighbor of 2 is node 1. What does the code do?
cards/10/goal/asks/0/explain: copy.ContainsKey(1) is true: 1′ was created at the very start. No new node is needed, but the copy needs the edge: 2′ must point to 1′. The edge 1 — 2 is two references, 1 → 2 and 2 → 1; from the side of 1 only the first was written. A second copy of 1 would split the graph: 2′ would point to a “1” that nobody else knows about.
cards/10/goal/asks/1/options/0/label: Only a reference: 3′ was created when 2 first met 3
cards/10/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: Creates 3′: node 3 has not been processed
cards/10/goal/asks/1/options/2/label: Skips it: 3 will add the 4′ → 3′ reference itself when it is taken
cards/10/goal/asks/1/q: 4 has been taken, and the reference to 1′ is added. The second neighbor is 3: it is still in the queue, nobody has looked at its neighbors. What does the code do?
cards/10/goal/asks/1/explain: A copy is created at the first meeting, not when the node leaves the queue: 3′ went into the dictionary while 2 was being processed. So for 4 the first-meeting branch does not fire — only 3′ goes into the neighbors of 4′. When 3 is taken, it adds the back references 3′ → 2′ and 3′ → 4′: each node fills only its own neighbor list.
cards/11/q: On a graph of two connected nodes 1 — 2 this code crashes with StackOverflowException. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/11/explain: The copy reaches the dictionary only after the neighbors are visited. Clone(1) creates a copy and goes into Clone(2); 2 points to 1, and 1 isn't in the dictionary yet — Clone(1) starts over, and so on forever. The line copy[node] = c must move up right after new Node: then Clone(1) called from Clone(2) returns the ready copy.
cards/12/q: You are solving Course Schedule out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: what the pair [a, b] means, whether there are duplicates and courses without prerequisites
cards/12/items/1: Reduce to a graph: the edge b → a; everything can be finished if there is no cycle
cards/12/items/2: Idea: Kahn — take courses with in-degree 0, decrement the in-degree of dependents
cards/12/items/3: Code: adjacency lists and in-degrees in O(V + E), a queue, a taken counter
cards/12/items/4: Run it on a diamond and on a small cycle 0 → 1 → 0
cards/12/items/5: Complexity: O(V + E) time and memory
cards/12/items/6: Variants: DFS with three colors, the order for #210, the order by ascending id
cards/12/explain: The direction of the pair is the main trap of the statement, so it is clarified first. Then the reduction to cycle detection, Kahn's idea, the code, a run on two graphs (the diamond checks in-degrees, the cycle checks the false answer), the cost and what else might be asked.
